Travel flows

Weekday commutes between Island places (Statistics Canada, 2021 Census) and trips to campuses, airports and ferries.
1001,00010,000 commuters
drivingby traincampus, airport, ferry· 1 dot ≈ 20 people
How this is estimatedWith E&N counts drivers whose home and work places are both near a passenger station (full share within 2 km, none beyond 8 km). “Every station, frequent” assumes all stations on the map get 16 or more trains a day each way; “Trains in this timetable” uses only the stations and trains in your plan, and shrinks the share where fewer than 16 trains a day link the two stations. Driving shares are estimated from each place's 2021 commutes; Statistics Canada rounds counts to 5 or 10. Arcs bend to the right of the direction of travel; the arrow points to the workplace. Moving travellers follow the quickest route on the main road network, timed by Census arrival-at-work times by region; the trip home is assumed 8.5 hours later. Traffic congestion: BC Ministry of Transportation count stations (2025 permanent and short counts) and City of Victoria counts by hour; local roads without counts are modelled from nearby population. With E&N, the drivers who switch are taken off the count stations on their route. Campuses: UVic's 2023 counted trips; Camosun and VIU scaled from UVic per student and staff member. Airports: 2024–25 passenger totals. Ferries: BC Ferries traffic for the year to March 2025, averaged over the year, timed by this fall's weekday sailings (drivers reach the terminal 10–60 minutes before a sailing and leave in the 20 minutes after one docks). Their trips are spread over places by population and travel time and are not shifted to rail. CRD 2022 survey: all trips made on a fall 2022 weekday by residents of the Capital Region, between 19 survey districts and two areas outside it (Tables 43–46 of the survey report); dots are timed by the survey's trips by hour of day. Driving shares per district pair are estimated from the survey's sub-area mode shares, transit from each district's transit trip total; the survey counts each direction separately, so switches are one-way trips.

Assumptions

  • Data-driven timetable on 8 trainsets: the Courtenay intercity (the ICF 05:54 and 16:51 trains) and two Nanaimo–Duncan–Victoria commuter trains (Nanaimo 05:30 and 06:05, back from Victoria 16:10 and 17:05) are placed first. West Shore trains then run both ways every 30 minutes from 05:30, every 15 minutes 06:30–09:00, every 20 minutes 09:00–14:00, every 10 minutes 14:00–16:00 (the afternoon peak starts early, with school trips), every 15 minutes 16:00–18:30 and every 30 minutes to 22:00, using the West Shore sets plus the regional sets while they wait in Victoria between peaks. Victoria departures are offset so layovers balance at both ends.
  • Data-driven timetable, unconstrained fleet: West Shore trains both ways every 30 minutes from 05:30, every 10 minutes 06:30–09:00 and 14:30–18:30 (sets that work the peaks run as two coupled units), every 15 minutes midday and every 30 minutes to 22:00. These are shaped by the CRD 2022 survey: West Shore ↔ core trips run both ways all day (about 46,000 a day each way, 36% counter-peak in the morning and 56% in the afternoon), the morning peak is sharp at 8 am and the afternoon peak runs 2–6 pm. Cowichan gets 4 commuter trains into Victoria arriving 06:45–08:30 and 4 back 15:30–17:45, plus a counter-peak run each way (3,095 Census commuters a day from the Cowichan Valley to Greater Victoria). A Duncan–Nanaimo shuttle runs 5 times each way (2,115 + 1,490 commuters a day between them), meeting Victoria trains at Duncan. Courtenay trains offer a morning arrival in Victoria, an evening return and day trips to Nanaimo.
  • ICF timetable: the service pattern from the Island Corridor Foundation business case (Tables 17 and 18), using its stop times. The West Shore line is tightened to a train every 12 minutes: Westhills → Victoria 06:00–15:00 and Victoria → Westhills 09:15–17:30. Trainsets out of position run back empty. Victoria ↔ Courtenay and Victoria ↔ Nanaimo have 3 trains a day each way; Duncan has 2 morning trains to Victoria and 2 afternoon trains back. Use the Timetable and Fleet tabs to change it.
  • Single track: a 12-minute service in both directions needs trains to pass every few minutes. That would require double track or several long passing loops between Victoria and Westhills, which this simulation does not model.
  • Run times for new or changed trips use track speeds of 90 km/h open line, 55 km/h on the Malahat, 45–60 km/h in Victoria and Nanaimo, and 40 km/h on the Port Alberni line, capped by each train type's top speed.
  • Trainsets turn around in 3 minutes and run empty to reposition when needed. Trains running in the same direction stay at least one signal block (1 km) apart and never overtake: a train that catches up waits at a signal and picks up the delay. Trains meeting head-on on single track are not modelled.
  • Highway traffic: BC Ministry of Transportation Traffic Data Program annual hourly day-of-week summaries (Monday–Friday averaged). Lane counts from OpenStreetMap; lane capacity assumed at 1,900 veh/h on freeway sections, 1,700 on highways with intersections, 1,400–1,500 on two-lane or arterial sections.
  • Road congestion dots: on highways the dot colour comes from the measured hourly counts above (green under 40% of estimated capacity, yellow 40–60%, red over 60%). Highway counts now include the 2025 Colwood interchange station (P-11-6NS) and twelve 2025 MoTI short counts on Highways 1, 14, 17, 19 and 19A, so segments between permanent stations use the nearest measured count. Roads with a public count are coloured from it: City of Victoria Open Data traffic counts (2019–2026, one-way daily volumes, spread over the day with the urban weekday profile; nearby sections of the same street share the count) and MoTI 2025 short counts on the Comox Valley Parkway and Brechin Road. Measured roads use about 800 veh/h per lane at signals (green under 45%, yellow 45–75%, red over). Every other local and connector road has no public count (Saanich, Langford, Colwood and Nanaimo publish none), so its colour is a modelled estimate: the weekday hourly shape of the urban count stations × how much population lives within a few kilometres (2021 Census) × road class. Hover a road to see whether it is measured or modelled. MoTI's segment AADT layer was not used because its values date from 2012.
  • Jobs: Statistics Canada 2021 Census, employed people by usual place of work (tables 98-10-0496 by census tract and 98-10-0495 by municipality); people who worked at home are listed but not placed on the map. Each tract's jobs are spread over its OpenStreetMap commercial, institutional and industrial land (weighted 1 : 0.6 : 0.4 per hectare). "Jobs within 800 m" counts that spread, so it is approximate. The 2021 Census ran during the pandemic, and 2026 place-of-work results are due in 2027.
  • Stations: new stations snap to the existing E&N alignment. Adding a stop to existing trips interpolates its time and adds 1 minute to later stops; removing a stop takes 1 minute off. Demand (0–10) sets how many riders a station generates.
  • Track: use the Track tab to drag the alignment or draw new track. When you move a section of existing track, the distance between its stations grows or shrinks with the new length, and run times follow. New track joins the line where you start drawing, gets a station at its far end, and runs at the design speed you choose. All track is treated as single track; trains meeting head-on are not simulated, so double track is not modelled. Changing track does not retime existing trips; trips that become too tight are flagged.
  • Map coverage: the whole of Vancouver Island, from Victoria to Port Hardy and Cape Scott, so track can be drawn to any part of it (use ▢ to see the whole island). Hillshade is computed at about 200 m and contours from a 400 m elevation grid (AWS Terrain Tiles, zoom 11), so very small landforms are smoothed. The mainland is shown flat and pale. North of Campbell River the map has highways (19, 28, 30), lakes, towns and population, but no local roads, trails, jobs or traffic counts.
